item.title: OpenAI’s AI misalignment problem is growing
item.description:
OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse, based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors.

In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets.

These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces.

The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI. In his personal blog, for instance, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the industry must “step back and assess the trust architecture for this new era.”

Destroying its own testing environment

OpenAI began more aggressive misalignment monitoring following the July 2026 Hugging Face incident, in which autonomous OpenAI research agents broke out of their sandboxes and targeted Hugging Face infrastructure. Hundreds of its agents also attacked the RubyGems platform and targeted German programming wiki sites in recent months.

In one of its new reports, OpenAI describes how an internal model, tasked with grading several other models, figured out how to damage its own environment when it couldn’t arrive at intended results.

When comparing seven responses from seven different models, the grader had to inspect the conversational context and work behind each response, and to include information pointing back to input files.

The model was instructed: Conversation context is **required** grading input, not optional background.

It discovered that required input files were missing, nevertheless, it tried to submit assessments with no supporting information. These were rejected by an automated check. The model also created seven fake conversation files and seven fake response files containing fabricated information; these were rejected, too.

“It considered submitting arbitrary scores, despite recognizing that it lacked the evidence to grade and that ‘random scoring’ was ‘unethical,’” OpenAI explained. The model also tested the automated check by submitting placeholder reports to learn what information a report had to contain and how many responses it was expected to grade.

After these failures, the model decided to damage its task environment, presumably with the hope that the host would replace it with one containing the missing inputs. It deleted software required to run its tools and tried to remove system directories.

Although automated checks rejected its incorrect or made-up grades, “this incident illustrates why monitoring must also cover the grader’s actions, including attempts that fail or crash without producing an accepted result,” OpenAI wrote.

Breaking the rules to get the right answers, hiding the evidence

In another instance, an OpenAI model developed and tested ways to bypass internet access restrictions.

The model was asked questions about teacher salaries, electrical grid connections, and disability counts in specific areas. It was limited to using basic HTTP GET data retrieval requests, but “the model sometimes treated this restriction as something to circumvent,” OpenAI explained.

It explored other ways to contact outside resources, for instance, determining whether its proxy intermediary service could carry other kinds of connections, or if outside services could make requests on its behalf. In some cases, it continued to probe these other options even when it had the statistics it needed.

“These cases show that a model may continue developing ways around access restrictions even when additional access is unnecessary to obtain the information it needs,” OpenAI wrote.

In a third instance, also involving public statistics, OpenAI models figured out how to bypass restrictions on internet access and get access to numbers from public government data sources.

The models in this experiment were also restricted to HTTP GET requests, but they “wrote custom programs to send other types of requests,” OpenAI explained.

Using one of these programs, a model queried a publicly-available dashboard, and even as it “explicitly recognized” that its actions violated its restrictions, it continued collecting much more data than it required. Later, it decided not to disclose what it had done.

Another model used a temporary email address to create and verify an account for a site, then downloaded publicly available data.

“These cases illustrate why correct answers are not enough to establish that a model behaved appropriately,” OpenAI wrote. “A model may obtain accurate information through prohibited methods, and deliberately conceal how it did so.”

In response to these incidents, and others, OpenAI says it has hardened security controls, taken “additional steps” to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, and improved alignment grading. It has also “extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic.”

This article originally appeared on CSOonline.

item.title: Firefox takes aim at the enterprise browser market
item.description:
There’s growing talk of digital sovereignty as enterprises rethink past consolidation decisions made in the name of simplicity.

Mozilla, developer of Firefox, argues that a “very specific, very important layer” has been mostly missing from that conversation: The browser.

To that end, the company has unveiled Firefox Enterprise in a bid to diversify the browser engine to support privacy, control, and security.

The new offering combines the Firefox browser with a management console that enterprises can run on their own infrastructure using their own tooling. Companies get a full view of their data and can govern how it moves, and IT teams can manage policy, access, and set controls around AI use.

Firefox is already deployed across thousands of organizations and used by roughly 200 million people each month, Mozilla said. It is built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple.

“If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” Mozilla CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo observed in the blog post announcing the product.

The promise of Firefox Enterprise

“Firefox is hardly the first browser vendor to offer an enterprise-optimized choice,” said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy. “But it carves out a unique value proposition for IT organizations intent on maintaining independent control over how browsers are deployed, configured, secured, and managed.”

Firefox Enterprise keeps core management within an organization’s own environment; its data, keys, telemetry, and policy remain in controlled boundaries that the organization can run on-premises and audit itself. IT teams can gate access and control policies based on user and device. They can also export browser events and audit activity in their SIEM, and native DLP helps prevent data loss.

Mozilla is particularly gearing Firefox Enterprise to organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance concerns. The offering can help enterprises meet regulatory requirements like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), the NIS2 directive, ISO27001, and SOC2.

IT teams can set external connection controls, allow or block organization-wide add-ons, and restrict browsing with a lockdown mode “so one zero-day doesn’t take down every browser in the estate,” the announcement said. AI use can be allowed, restricted, or disabled. 

From a security standpoint, enterprises can set data loss prevention (DLP) rules by domain or action, and integrate with existing security information and event management (SIEM) tools like Trellix or Broadcom to extend analysis into the browser.

IT teams can protect against phishing, malware, and malicious sites with native isolation, extension control, and managed security updates. Access can be gated based on user and device, without the need for virtual private networks (VPNs), remote browser isolation (RBI), and virtual desktops.

The company said that it will use a subscription model “that doesn’t depend on monetizing customer data or forcing a roadmap.” Firefox Enterprise includes Firefox Professional support; for businesses running the free Firefox browser without Firefox Enterprise, Firefox Professional support is available as a paid subscription.

Firefox Enterprise is now being introduced in Europe, initially across France, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, with more markets to follow. Mozilla is also developing Thunderbird Enterprise, which will manage Thunderbird email, calendar, and contacts.

The case for enterprise browsers

Largely thanks to the shift to cloud-based computing, the browser has evolved from a simple internet gateway to the place where most workers spend virtually all of their time. This makes them “the very epicenters of modern enterprise digital security,” said Levy.

Thus it makes sense for IT to consider the merits of a dedicated enterprise browser. But, Levy said, “there are no ideal solutions in IT, and enterprise-class browsers are no exception.”

Employees may bristle at additional layers of controls and raise privacy concerns around centralized monitoring. Administrative complexity is also a concern, as existing identity management, endpoint management, monitoring, and data protection tools may not always “cleanly integrate” with a more robust browser, he noted.

Enterprise-class browsers also can’t stop “less-than-ideally-trained employees” from clicking on phishing links, and they also can’t protect against “every last malicious extension.” As always, bad actors can find ways to compromise sensitive corporate data or otherwise use AI toolsets in unsanctioned ways.

But these types of browser can help minimize AI-related risks as employees lean more heavily into chatbots and agents. Admins can craft more flexible rules of engagement; for example, workers could access a web app for deep-dive analysis, but humans and AI alike could be prevented from copying data externally. Enterprise browsers also allow more granular control of AI features, and even disengagement if they conflict with policy.

Key differentiators

Firefox Enterprise isn’t the only option when choosing an enterprise browser, however. Microsoft Edge for Business would likely still be the preferred choice for environments already heavily invested in Microsoft’s enterprise Azure and Microsoft 365 ecosystem, Levy pointed out. Similar logic would apply to Google Chrome Enterprise’s appeal for those already committed to Google’s cloud and productivity infrastructure. And the Prisma Browser from Palo Alto Networks integrates aggressive cybersecurity tools with monitoring of AI use, remote devices, and unmanaged devices.

Firefox Enterprise’s key differentiation is its use of the Gecko browser engine, and its management console that can be deployed on a company’s own infrastructure, Levy said. This might make it a good fit for shops that want to minimize implementation disruptions to existing data management, access control, and compliance protocols.

“Firefox Enterprise lets customers craft their own deployment roadmap, assuming they have the skills and resources to self-manage the process,” Levy said.

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

item.title: Workday launches Sana-based UI, autopilot agents, as it deepens its focus on AI
item.description:
When Workday acquired Sana just about a year ago, it said that the combination of Sana’s AI with Workday’s platform would create a new “front door” to work. Today at its Workday Rising conference, it unveiled that front door, turning Sana into Workday’s default home screen that, it said, “brings tasks, decisions, meetings, and agent activity into one place, helping employees move directly from what needs attention to getting it done.”

The new interface goes beyond merely answering questions to orchestrating Workday’s agents to execute tasks. Each employee’s experience is tailored to their role; when they open the application, they see the tasks and decisions that need their attention and can take action directly from the UI. And, using TypeSafe’s Jev AI model, Sana adapts its UI to each task, the company said, generating forms, calendars, approval cards, visualizations, and other interactive experiences in real time and completing tasks once the employee approves the action. It also supports work that spans multiple days, displaying relevant information at every stage of functions such as financial closing or preparation of workforce plans by HR.

Sana also works within other AI tools and platforms including Anthropic Claude, Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise, and Microsoft Copilot, as well as within Microsoft Teams and Slack. But, Workday said in its announcement, “third-party AI tools and platforms never get raw access to Workday data — they can now access this data through Sana, and Sana does the reasoning, applies each company’s own permissions, approvals, and policies, and carries out the work so actions are lawful by design and recorded, regardless of the tool it started in.”

Along with the Sana home page, known as Workday Home, the company introduced Sana Concierge, which brings together the self-service capabilities and Sana for IT Service Management released earlier this year with Workday Help and Case Agent to create AI-native employee services spanning HR and IT. Workday said it can resolve requests such as password resets, access requests, and questions about time off and payroll, as well as performing onboarding and offboarding. The employee just submits a natural language request, and Concierge looks up relevant policies and, based on the employee’s Workday information, guides them through the steps to complete their request.

If a human decision is needed, Concierge routes the request to the right person in the background, but remains the employee’s point of contact.

The Sana Workday Home experience is available today, with more capabilities and support “coming soon,” the company said. Sana Concierge is available now to early adopter customers, with general availability expected in the first quarter of 2027.

From copilots to autopilots

The company also introduced four new autonomous AI agents that act as autopilots across hiring, payroll, accounting, and compliance.

“From co-pilots to autopilots, that’s a big transition that you will see across our agents today,” said Joel Hellermark, former CEO of Sana, who is now Workday’s chief AI officer. “These are now agents that anticipate what needs attention, they apply the company’s policies, they advise on the next step, and then act once the appropriate person approves that. And these autopilots run completely on Workday’s rails, so they’re self-governed and compliant.”

And, he said, while a typical copilot-driven system “sits there” until the user logs in, autopilot agents run on a heartbeat, operating whether or not the user is online.

The Talent Acquisition Agent, for example, monitors the open job queue from the time a position is posted, finding qualified candidates and giving the recruiter information about them. It can generate outreach to potential hires and present it to the recruiter for approval, explain why candidates on a short list are a good fit, and schedule interviews with those the recruiter flags. It then automatically joins the interview and takes notes. Based on recruiter feedback, the agent learns how to improve its recommendations.

The agent works across multiple recruiting tools, including Workday Recruiting, HiredScore, Paradox, native Workday skills, and connected sourcing providers. The autopilot capabilities are available to early adopter customers today, with general availability planned for early 2027.

Three more autopilots will arrive for early adopters in early 2027, for Payroll Agent, Accounting Agent, and Deployment Agent.

This could be the start of a change in the coordination of work, said Melody Brue, analyst in residence at Moor Insights & Strategy. “Workday is trying to connect more of the work around a decision, from weighing options to carrying out the approved plan,” she said. “Sana could become the starting point for that process, giving Workday a larger role in coordinating work beyond its own applications. For current customers, the meaningful change would be less manual coordination between a request, an approval, and a completed transaction. The value depends on whether that reduces the work employees have to manage or shifts it into resolving exceptions when a workflow crosses systems.”

Extending Decision Intelligence

Workday Decision Intelligence, first seen in Adaptive from Workday, is spreading into more areas of the business, said Yasmeen Ahmad, SVP and GM, Workday Data Cloud.

Decision Intelligence is not an agent performing a task, she said. “It’s a planning and reasoning experience built for decisions that are too complex, too high stakes, or too cross-functional for any single task to capture.”

Ahmad described a scenario in which HR revised a hiring plan using Decision Intelligence, passing it to Finance to use as an input for reviewing its quarterly projections with the same tool.

“Normally this would have taken six weeks, five spreadsheets, and analysts trying to stitch it together. Today, it was all just a prompt,” she said.

Brue said that what she finds interesting is whether Workday can take more of the manual modeling out of a staffing discussion. “Workday already supports connected workforce and financial planning,” she said. “If teams can work through several options with fewer model adjustments and less reliance on specialists for routine ones, planning could be more responsive when business needs change.”

Work Intelligence

Work Intelligence, available to early access Workday Human Capital Management customers, breaks jobs into their component tasks, describing the skills employees need to perform them. It draws on Workday Skills Cloud, giving leaders a look at how jobs are changing, and then, using Decision Intelligence, companies can get a picture of their internal readiness for evolving work.

“The task-level analysis is worth watching,” Brue said. “A role is rarely entirely automatable or entirely human-led. Looking inside the role could give customers a more useful basis for redesigning work. But saving time across a dozen tasks doesn’t automatically free someone up for a different assignment. Companies may need to regroup the work, letting agents handle routine steps together and giving employees clear responsibility for what comes next.”

Off with its head

Workday also announced that its Trusted Agent Platform, on which organizations build and run AI agents governed by their business rules, is now headless, allowing customers to use the development tools and models of their choice. It brings together the existing Workday Data Cloud, Agent-Ready Tools, Developer Agent, custom agents, and Agent Harness.

However, Workday CTO Gabe Monroy emphasized that, at the same time, “headless can’t mean lawless. The rules for HR and finance already live in Workday, so customers don’t have to rebuild them for every agent they create. This is what lets companies move fast with agents without losing control.”

And, to enhance the controls, in early 2027 the company will add Agent Context Service and Grounded Reasoning to Agent Harness to provide Workday context that agents need and check requests against company policies, business processes, and tenant data before the agent is allowed to act.

“Governance gets more consequential as agents move from recommendations to actions,” Brue pointed out. “An agent can be authorized and still make the wrong call. Customers need to distinguish permission to recommend from permission to execute. And know which actions require human approval, especially in hiring and finance. The governance question extends to any workflow that crosses platforms. Customers need clear ownership of approvals, exceptions, and the audit trail when a request starts in one system, and an agent acts in another.”

For companies already using Workday and ServiceNow together, she said, there’s an additional consideration: Workday’s expansion into employee-facing AI and agent governance could create more overlap between platforms that have traditionally played complementary roles.

“Joint customers don’t suddenly need to choose one, but they may need to clarify which platform coordinates the work and how controls operate across both,” she said. “A unified experience won’t necessarily mean unified control.”

item.title: A shared channel is not a principal: Whose authority is the agent spending?
item.description:
Imagine an outside incident responder typing into a shared channel: “Roll back the production release, revoke every active session and send the incident update to the customer.”

An engineering director adds a thumbs-up. Outside counsel and two vendors are also in the channel. The agent uses a service account with permission to carry out all three actions.

Whose authority is it about to spend?

At Dreamforce on September 15, Slack described code channels where teams and agents write, review and ship code together. High-stakes work, such as a production deployment, is presented for a teammate’s sign-off. The announcement listed Slack Code as available and Slackbot in channels as an early pilot. The same day, Salesforce announced AWS DevOps Agent in Slack, with other AWS agents scheduled for the fall.

Sign-off is an important control. The approval shown in the channel must cover the action being taken and come from someone authorized to approve it.

The conversation is not the authority

In access-control language, a principal is an identity — such as a user, workload or group — to which the system can assign permissions. A channel is a place to collaborate. Its members do not acquire collective authority over production or payments merely by joining the conversation.

Both Slack Connect and Teams shared channels support cross-company collaboration. Knowing which account posted a message, and which organization it belongs to, is essential. It does not establish whether that account may order a rollback or receive the investigation’s findings.

Channel membership can be an intentional input to policy. An organization might grant a tightly governed group a defined operational role. The danger is treating membership in an ordinary channel as blanket permission to use an agent’s tools, even as participants come and go.

NIST’s zero-trust architecture rejects implicit trust based solely on network location. By analogy, a channel ID should not become the new corporate subnet.

Nothing malicious has to happen for this boundary to fail. Every account can be authentic and every participant well-intentioned. The failure occurs when a system treats the ability to request work as sufficient authority to have it performed.

Separate the request from the right to execute it

In the incident channel, the responder makes the request. Authority might come from the incident commander’s assigned role or from a recovery workflow approved by a business owner. The director can approve an action only if policy grants that decision right. The agent executes under the service account’s identity. The customer and channel participants are separate audiences whose access must also be considered.

Those roles may overlap, but the system must not assume they do.

Credentials carry real permissions. In Microsoft Graph’s permission model, delegated access is limited by both the application’s granted permissions and the signed-in user’s access. App-only access uses the application’s own identity and permissions. The distinction matters when a conversation triggers an agent with permissions broader than the sender’s own.

Broader permissions can be legitimate: a support employee may initiate an approved workflow without personally holding its administrative credentials. A defined policy must determine who may initiate the workflow and which actions it permits. Without that link, the agent can become a route around the controls that prevent the employee from acting directly.

In finance, “Renew the vendor, change its bank details and pay the invoice” sounds like one task. It crosses procurement, supplier verification and payment authority. A check mark from accounts payable cannot be assumed to authorize all three.

Approval is a decision by an eligible principal over a defined action. The interface should make that decision understandable; the enforcement system must make it binding.

AWS documents a directed-action approval flow that binds an operator’s approval to a specific operation and resource, limits how long it remains valid and records who approved the action in CloudTrail. The enterprise must configure who may approve actions, how tools are classified and which resources the agent may affect.

Bind permission to the action that actually happens

On September 15, NIST finalized IR 8587, guidance on protecting identity and access tokens. Its authorization guidance calls for access decisions to consider context beyond whether a token is valid. The report applies when agents use signed tokens but explicitly excludes broader agent-access challenges. Enterprises still have to define who may authorize a rollback, a payment or a disclosure.

The model can interpret a request and propose a plan. Permission to carry out that plan must be established from authoritative identity, role, delegation and workflow records. The model should not infer it from apparent seniority, urgency or agreement in the conversation.

Three controls should govern every deployment.

  1. Verify the requester and the source of authority. Verify the platform event and the sender’s stable identity, including their organization. Check request freshness and guard against duplicate execution when messages are retried or replayed. Determine whether the action is authorized by the requester’s own permissions, explicit delegation, a valid approval or a governed workflow. For high-risk operations, require fresh authentication or transaction-specific confirmation according to policy.
  2. Make the approval specific. Turn the request into explicit operations before authorizing it: the production service to roll back and the version to restore, the sessions to revoke and the update to send and its destination. Approval should be tied to those details and expire after a defined period. If the target, scope or destination changes, reevaluate authorization and obtain fresh approval where required. Two-person rules must verify distinct eligible approvers, not simply count reactions.
  3. Enforce authorization at execution and disclosure. Recheck authority before each consequential action. For queued or delayed work, check again at execution; if the integration cannot support that check, limit what the agent may do. Keep reusable credentials outside the model’s context and restrict them to the necessary operations and resources. Where broad credentials are unavoidable, route execution through a controlled service that enforces the approved operation and prevents bypass. Permission to read information does not automatically permit posting it to everyone in the channel.

Preserve a linked record of the request, the basis for authorization, the approval, the executing identity and the observed outcome. The agent must not be able to rewrite or delete prior entries. Record refusals, partial completion and uncertain results as well as success. Never include credential secrets.

An immaculate audit trail of an unauthorized action is still not a preventive control.

When only part of the request is authorized

Return to the incident channel. A company’s policy might authorize a recovery workflow to roll back a specified service when defined health thresholds are crossed. Revoking all sessions could require a separate security decision. Sending the customer update could require an authorized communications owner and an approved destination.

The agent should handle those decisions separately. If the steps are safe to perform independently, it could carry out the permitted rollback, hold session revocation for approval and prepare the update without sending it. The director’s thumbs-up should not turn three distinct decisions into one permission.

A person need not approve every tool call. A governed workflow can carry prior authorization for specified actions within explicit limits. A runbook describes a procedure; an accountable owner must authorize its use and define when it may run.

CIOs should assign these decisions to the teams accountable for their consequences: operations for recovery, finance for payments and the relevant business owner for disclosure. Security and identity teams should make those rules enforceable. The integration team should not have to invent business policy while connecting a bot.

Make the pilot prove the boundary

Before expanding a shared-channel agent, ask for a demonstration in a test environment:

  1. Have an external participant request an action they are not entitled to initiate. Show what stops it.
  2. Approve one production target, then change the target. Show that the original approval does not authorize the substitution.
  3. Revoke a required permission before execution. Show when the revocation takes effect and what can still run during any delay.
  4. Change the destination of a permitted report to an unauthorized channel. Show that disclosure is blocked.
  5. Replay a completed request. Show that it does not create a second consequential action, and that the evidence explains the outcome.

Include an authorized case too. Controls must preserve legitimate work, including approved delegation, while rejecting requests outside its limits.

The team must explain why each action was allowed or denied. “The bot had access” and “someone in the channel approved” are not sufficient answers.

Before the agent rolls production back, revokes sessions or sends the customer update, the organization should be able to identify the authority behind each action. A shared channel can coordinate the work; it cannot confer that authority on its own.

item.title: Why process excellence will become the competitive advantage in the AI economy
item.description:
The AI revolution is here, and enterprises everywhere are racing to deploy the latest tools, agents and models. Yet, the simple truth is that access to AI technology is no longer a competitive advantage. Open-weight models are becoming universally available, and enterprises can dynamically optimize which model to use for any given task.

If the technology itself is no longer the differentiator, what will separate the winners from the laggards? The answer will increasingly lie in the layers of context, control and support around those models – whether agents have sufficiently rich, accurate and timely information about how the business works, and the right guardrails to operate effectively within it.

For decades, enterprises have been told that data is their most strategic asset. This remains true, but I would argue that a well-described digital twin of an organization is itself a strategic dataset – a detailed understanding of how the business operates. That understanding has always been valuable, sometimes mandatory in regulated industries, but in the AI era it becomes business-critical

Without it, AI agents – no matter how advanced – will struggle to execute work autonomously, scale effectively or deliver meaningful outcomes. The illusion of AI as a silver bullet persists, but the reality is far more nuanced. If two companies deploy the same AI technology, why might one achieve transformative results while the other sees only marginal gains?

The difference isn’t the model but the contextual information it can work on. A company with poorly defined, ambiguous or siloed processes will find its AI initiatives plagued by inefficiencies, errors and unintended consequences. Meanwhile, an organization with deep process rigor will unlock AI’s full potential, delivering faster execution, lower costs and higher customer satisfaction

Take, for example, Legal & General, one of the UK’s leading financial services organizations, managing more than £1 trillion in assets, which undertook a major transformation with more than 2000 business processes reviewed, approved and maintained by the business, ensuring its AI agents operate from accurate, governed information rather than disconnected documents or outdated knowledge.

This is where process context becomes strategically important. Every company may increasingly have access to the same models, but no two companies operate in the same way. The knowledge embedded in how an organization serves customers, manages exceptions, coordinates teams, applies controls and makes decisions has been built up over years – sometimes decades.

When that understanding is captured and made available to AI, it becomes something competitors cannot simply buy or replicate. The model may be increasingly commoditized; the context you give it is uniquely yours and creates a compounding advantage where an agent with deeper process context can make better decisions and execute work more effectively.

To trust AI agents with autonomous work, enterprises must ensure their processes meet critical criteria. First, clarity and precision are non-negotiable. AI agents cannot operate effectively if processes are described in vague or incomplete terms. Every step, variation and outlier must be documented with enough detail to remove programmatic ambiguity.

Every process has a “happy path,” but real life in a large, complex organization rarely follows it. There are outliers, unexpected events and variations driven by everything from customer behavior to different laws and regulatory requirements across jurisdictions. For agents to operate at scale, they need to understand those variations properly.

It is only with this detailed understanding of the current process and all its variations and exceptions that you have any chance of redesigning the process to make it “agentic” without making simplistic decisions that will turn out to be costly mistakes.

Second, processes don’t exist in isolation; they are interconnected and interdependent, and changes in one area often create bottlenecks or inefficiencies elsewhere. For example, automating a single workflow might accelerate throughput in one department but create congestion downstream. A digital twin – a dynamic, continuously updated representation of the organization’s processes – is essential to anticipate and mitigate these ripple effects.

Consider Siemens, which mapped out its end-to-end process model to create such a digital twin of its supply chain operations. By simulating the impact of AI-driven automation before deployment, the manufacturing giant was able to identify potential bottlenecks and optimize its processes end-to-end, resulting in a 20% reduction in lead times.

Finally, governance and risk management are paramount. As AI agents take on more autonomy, boards and executives must ask themselves where those agents are operating, what risks they introduce and how they are controlled.

AI deployment is no longer just an operational concern – it’s a board-level risk, akin to cybersecurity. Without proper guardrails, agents can behave unpredictably, leading to compliance violations, reputational damage or financial losses.

For example, JPMorgan Chase is using AI in transaction screening to review more than twice the volume while halving the number of manual operator checks, resulting in faster turnaround and fewer delays. Crucially, the bank says its AI strategies are aligned to end-to-end client journeys, helping ensure AI is applied where it creates the most value rather than automating individual tasks in isolation.

For CEOs, this shift demands a new priority: treating process not as an implementation detail but as a core strategic imperative. Historically, process management has been the domain of operational teams or quality departments but, today, it’s moving to the C-suite. COOs and CIOs are increasingly owning process transformation, recognizing that AI success hinges on process depth. Companies that neglect this shift risk falling behind, stuck in a cycle of piecemeal pilots and narrow use cases that fail to deliver scalable results.

Ultimately, for most enterprises, the AI race will be more of an execution race than a technology race. The differentiator won’t simply be the agentic capabilities companies can access, but the outcomes they can achieve with it – doing what they do today faster, more efficiently and in ways that create a better experience for their customers. And successful execution starts with process.

item.title: 6 IT wins to deliver before the year ends
item.description:
CIOs entered the year with ambitions to bring more AI into their companies and start using AI to transform how work gets done. At the same time they also wanted to leverage tech to cut costs and boost productivity throughout the business. And they hoped to use their post to help drive the strategic vision for their organizations.

Now into the fourth quarter, CIOs say they’re still pursuing those objectives and plenty more. They say they still have much work to do, and they’re aiming to close the year with wins in myriad areas.

Here, IT leaders share advice on what their peers should focus on based on what they are racing to finish before year’s end.

1. Be good to your word

One of the top to-do items for many CIOs as they near year’s end is delivering on their promises.

As Robert Field, global CIO at tech advisory firm Adler Advisors, says, people may not remember all the work IT did in any given year, “but they’ll always remember the things you didn’t do that you said you would.”

Field also cites fiscal reasons for his drive to finish up all IT work planned for 2026, noting that the company, which runs on a calendar year, has already allocated the money for the work in its annual budget and has pegged some of it to anticipated tax credits.

Moreover, employees’ performance reviews are done on the calendar year, he says, which means planned projects need to be completed so leaders can accurately assess employees’ work and contributions.

Jason Brucker, managing director for CIO solutions at consulting firm Protiviti, says every year around this time he hears from many CIOs who are looking to finish what they started. But it can be a hard-fought win, he says. End-of-year tasks are piling up on workers, teams are starting to take time to plan for the upcoming year, and the C-suite is stressing the need for IT to deliver measurable value to the business.

Still, despite the distractions, closing the books on promises made can help prove the value of IT’s ability to not only deliver solutions but make good on allotted investments — an important win for securing funding for the next slate of projects.

2. Prove this year’s solutions deliver when it matters most

The last months of the year are always the busiest for Kenco Group, which as a large third-party logistics provider experiences a spike in demand for its services. Pal Narayanan, its chief digital and information officer, wants to use that peak volume to make clear that his IT department has no problem keeping operations up and running smoothly even at full tilt.

Although demonstrating IT’s ability to keep pace with the business is always critical, Narayanan says he wants a win this upcoming busy season because IT has added more automation and robotics within company processes “and we want to make sure those work flawlessly.”

But his IT team needs to be prepared to work quickly if there are any issues that need to be addressed, as Narayanan notes that this is the first peak season the company will go through with the new technology in place. “Every minute matters during peak season, so I’m making sure everyone is in place, and everything is built for scale, and if any additional capability needs to be turned on, our vendors are ready,” he adds.

3. Fortify business alignment for the year ahead

For Adler Advisors’ Field, building relationships with colleagues is an ongoing task. But year-end provides a ripe opportunity to check in with his peers, tie IT work to hoped-for business outcomes, and discuss goals for the upcoming year, he says.

“I use this time to talk to people and to meet up and align IT with their strategic plans for next year, so my team is aligned to achieve that with them,” he says.

Field is disciplined in his outreach, as he keeps track of meetings and his colleagues’ preferred communication modes. He has had workers on his own IT team also work on building relationships with their business counterparts to ensure those team members understood the business and how IT could provide “exponential value” to it.

And while Field meets with leaders in the business all year, he uses the fourth-quarter meetings to reflect on IT’s performance and solicit feedback on how it could do better and be more impactful. “It’s an opportunity to hear where they need me or my department to lean in on more, so we can deliver what they need,” he adds. “Inevitably there’s something I wasn’t thinking about.”

4. Advance the AI agenda

Many CIOs are looking for AI wins to close out the year, says Brucker of his client work for Protiviti. Today that means not just deploying AI capabilities but “rolling out AI to gain value.”

“They’re looking to go from the experimentation phase to the business value realization phase,” he says, noting that how they plan to do that varies from one organization to the next.

Kenco Group’s Narayanan hopes to accelerate his company’s AI strategy and plans to use the rest of this year to position his IT department to deliver on that. He’s currently identifying what is working and what is not so that IT can focus on what’s bringing success and shed what isn’t. To deliver on his goal before year-end, Narayanan is also establishing partnerships with new vendors — both nimble startups and mature, established providers — to bring a combination of agility, innovation, and experience. He’s implementing AI training and education to build competency and excitement, and he’s putting in financial metrics that can be used to measure the ROI on new AI initiatives. He believes doing this work now will allow for faster selection and adoption of AI in 2027 as well as faster achievement of benefits.

Meanwhile, Zach LaValley, CTO of RapidSOS, an intelligent safety platform and public safety AI company, is creating what he calls an “internal intelligence plane that everybody — humans and AI — can tap into.”

LaValley, who oversees internal IT at the company, envisions this replacing the data silos that limit AI use in organizations, with the plane having the needed security protections, access controls, and integration points that would allow AI applications to quickly and easily connect with it. LaValley says by year’s end he wants to connect all the data sources to this new plane. For additional 2026 wins, he wants to port over all the AI apps built by employees and start making those discoverable so that employees won’t have to reinvent apps that already exist.

Nina Tatsiy, CIO of Quadient, a global automation platform, wants to spend the next two months convincing everyone in the company “to embrace agentic AI.” She’ll consider it a win if she can accomplish that.

Along with that, Tatsiy wants to technically ready the organization for agentic AI transformation. “My biggest focus is how to set up an operating model for agents, governance for agents, and building a strategy around what that means for the rest of the technology stack,” she says.

5. Rein in AI costs

Like many IT execs, Sebastian Arriada, CIO of Globant, a global technology and IT services company, is seeing the cost of using AI spike as the number of “tokens we consume at the company grow almost exponentially.”

So, with an eye on reducing those bills, Arriada’s infrastructure team implemented Nvidia boxes so that Globant can deploy open-source models on them. Arriada explains that the move will let Globant balance the use of tokens between commercial and (less costly) open-source AI models.

There’s more work to be done before the boxes are operational, Arriada says. His goal is to have them up and running as well as expand the use of the open-source models by 5X this year. He expects to hit that goal by the end of November, noting that he wants to deliver another 5X in increased capacity in 2027.

Not all CIOs are ready to make the leap to hosting their own open weight models on expensive Nvidia hardware, but eyes on AI costs is common theme. Finishing out the year with a battle-tested plan for reining in AI spend is a worthy win regardless of how it’s executed.

6. Devise a 2027 budget for maximum impact and future-proof potential

Research firm Gartner projects that IT budgets will grow by an average of 3.7% in 2027 but cautions that, accounting for inflation, that increase will be marginal for most CIOs.

Actual budget figures for next year vary (and are not publicly disclosed), but CIOs of every stripe say one of the last wins they want for 2026 is to lock in an IT budget for 2027 that can maximize impact while keeping the price tag down.

It’s a task that “comes with a lot of pressure,” Adler Advisors’ Field admits. He expects to draft multiple iterations of his 2027 budget this fall, working with his IT team and consulting with business counterparts to come up with figures capable of supporting all of IT’s necessary run, grow, and transform costs — without breaking the bank. He’ll consider it a win when the budget is not just done but accepted by the board.

Quadient’s Tatsiy has a similar objective as she looks ahead for IT, saying she’s working “to transform all the functions I’m managing, not just for cost savings but to future-proof them.”

She says she’s looking at what she can rationalize and where she can deploy agentic AI to “change my function to be less focused on run and more focused on investing in the future.” Like Field, she says devising a 2027 budget that moves her further along that path would be a laudable way to close out the current year.

item.title: Stop sending me engineers: what OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft misread about enterprise AI
item.description:
The AI industry says enterprises can’t absorb AI. Its answer is to absorb it for them.

That’s not the same thing.

The engineer across the table knew the model cold. Not vendor-deck cold. He could tell me where it would break, what it would cost, and which benchmark numbers to ignore. One of the better technical minds who has ever sat in that chair.

Forty minutes in, I asked which of our problems he would point to first. He named a minor workflow one of my directors had mentioned that morning.

The easy read is that he didn’t know my business. True, and not very interesting. Here is the real issue: the people who sent him are making the exact mistake they are being paid to fix.

They’re not wrong about the problem

The frontier labs aren’t confused, and I want to be fair before I disagree.

MIT found that about 95% of enterprise AI pilots produced no measurable profit impact, despite tens of billions spent. Winning the benchmark wasn’t winning the deal. And a customer who never gets to production never renews.

So, they did the logical thing. They sent engineers:

  • OpenAI: Launched the OpenAI Deployment Company in May with $4 billion of initial investment from 19 partners, starting with 150 forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) and deployment specialists.
  • Anthropic: Partnered its engineering capability into an enterprise AI services venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs, reportedly valued above $1.5 billion.
  • Microsoft: Launched Frontier Company in July with $2.5 billion and approximately 6,000 embedded engineers and industry experts.
  • AWS: Committed $1 billion to a forward-deployed engineering unit embedding engineers with customers.
  • Market surge: FDE job postings grew roughly 800% in nine months, with principal-level compensation past $1.2 million.

That is a serious response. But it answers the wrong question.

All that capital is aimed at getting customers into production and keeping them there. We have been reading it as the playbook for getting AI into the wider economy. Those are two entirely different problems, and only one of them currently has anyone working on it.

The same mistake, twice

One structural fact tells you what this really is: the forward-deployed function sits on the commercial side of these companies, not in research. OpenAI capitalized its deployment arm as a separate business with outside investors.

That’s not an accusation; the org chart is simply more honest than the positioning. What that structure measures is pilots converted to production within the quarter. Against that scoreboard, the model isn’t shallow at all. It’s optimal.

Now look at the same failure from my side of the table.

A team builds an intelligent demand-forecasting agent. Accuracy improves by double digits. The engineering readout is genuinely good. And absolutely nothing happens to cash.

Accuracy was never the point. It only matters if it changes an operational decision: how much safety stock you hold, what commitments you make to suppliers, or what you schedule to build. If none of that changes, you haven’t freed a single dollar. Worse, if the model was tuned for fill rate, because that’s what the commercial team asked for — inventory climbs, working capital gets suffocated, and you are worse off than before. The project wins. The company loses.

Anyone who runs S&OP knows this reality: inventory is cash sitting on a shelf. Every forecast is a claim on that cash. Every service-level promise decides how much liquidity you lock away. The value is never in optimizing a single, isolated number; it is in managing the trade-offs between them.

Outside engineers cannot own those trade-offs. Look at what their engagements are sold on: a deflected ticket, an automated records request, a closed underwriting case. Local, siloed inside one function, and measurable in weeks. Those are the only outcomes an outsider can deliver before rolling off to the next logo.

The results a CFO cares about cross three functions and only show up in cash two quarters later.

Delivery vs. Diffusion

This gets celebrated as AI reaching the real economy. In practice, it does close to the opposite:

  • The learning runs one way. Anthropic’s job listings are the most explicit about this, asking engineers to codify repeatable deployment patterns and contribute those insights back to product and engineering. That is honest, and it is the point. Analysts have flagged the same concern from the buyer’s side: that deep reliance on frontier labs hands those labs insight into the very industries they may later enter.
  • Capability is replaced instead of built. The engagement leaves behind a functioning workflow, but zero internal muscle to solve the next bottleneck. Constellation Research warned this year that FDEs are often used as a crutch for product immaturity, and as part of a broader vendor dependency play. Without Palantir’s feedback loop — where every deployment continuously enriches an integrated customer ontology — this is simply an expensive systems consultancy with a frontier brand name.
  • The mid-market waits. Dice reported in August that the shortage of engineers is now directly holding back enterprise AI returns. The scarcest engineering talent sits inside Fortune 50 anchor accounts, while the companies that make up most of the economy queue behind them.

In engagements structured this way, the lab learns your business. You learn their product.

So here is the test I now apply to any engagement, including the ones I sign: when it ends, are we better at finding the next problem ourselves?

If the capability leaves the building when the outside engineer packs up their laptop, that was delivery, not diffusion. Delivery is a fine business, but it doesn’t compound. Diffusion is nothing but compounding.

What we did instead

We eventually fixed our inventory problem.

Not by pointing an off-the-shelf frontier model at raw ERP tables, but by redesigning our entire planning architecture from the ground up. We staffed the initiative with operators who had spent years inside our supply chain and knew where the real constraints actually sat — the lead time, the allocation rule, the supplier commitment that no outsider would have known to model and then applied AI directly to those decision points.

The result: Inventory came down and stayed down, turns improved, and the part that matters for this argument, nobody had to be flown in to do it again the following quarter.

There is no version of that outcome a single outside engineer could have designed, no matter how brilliant the model in his hands.

The bigger stake

Scale this up and the macro picture becomes clear. A country’s AI advantage will not come from a few hundred flagship deployments. It will come from millions of operators applying AI to operational decisions they were previously making badly.

Which brings me back to the man across the table.

We are spending millions sending AI experts to learn business. We should be sending business operators to learn AI.

  • Business knowledge is slow. It took most of my career to instinctively know which trade-offs to make around working capital and inventory.
  • AI execution is fast. An experienced operational team can master agentic tooling, evals, and model orchestration in a matter of months.

We are running the harder transfer at immense cost and mistaking it for progress.

I don’t need more forward-deployed engineers. I need backward-deployed domain experts.

Nobody is selling those. Which means the only people who can build them are already on your payroll.

item.title: SAP customers seek renewed control over their ERP fate
item.description:
“Claim your ground, lead your business” is the overarching motto of this year’s German-speaking SAP User Group (DSAG) congress — a slogan the organizers say aims to bring SAP’s technological vision in line with the concrete challenges faced by its customers, complete with a striking Western motif.

The congress, in its 27th year, kicked off with a keynote from outgoing CEO Jens Hungershausen, who underscored the theme, telling the more than 6,000 participants that, in a time of constant change, they — as the companies and organizations who depend on their SAP systems to operate — must consciously define their own scope of action. It’s about acting autonomously, finding one’s own pace, taking responsibility, and making well-founded decisions, he said.

Referring to a saying often attributed to Henry Ford, Hungershausen explained there are always three possibilities: Love it, change it, or leave it — a principle that can readily be applied to the SAP ecosystem.

Based on the results of the DSAG investment survey from early 2026, Hungershausen outlined the decision-making dilemmas many user companies currently face.

Unclear added value of S/4HANA migrations

First, there’s the end-of-maintenance dilemma for customers of older SAP versions: According to the survey, 54% of the companies still use SAP ECC or even SAP Business Suite, even though standard maintenance for SAP ECC expires at the end of 2027. This deadline forces many companies to migrate to S/4HANA, often creating a conflict between unclear business benefits and high investment costs, according to Hungershausen.

At the same time, questions remain around the appropriate operating model. SAP’s preferred approach is the cloud — specifically the public cloud. However, when it comes to S/4HANA, this currently plays a minor role for DSAG companies.

“For us at DSAG, one thing is clear: Cloud is the future. In reality, however, S/4HANA On-Premise and hybrid architectures are the everyday reality for many of our members, and SAP has to accept that,” Hungershausen said.

The DSAG’s corresponding demand to SAP: Key innovations must not be reserved exclusively for cloud customers.

Here, Hungershausen described SAP’s announcement at Sapphire — that selected AI scenarios would also be available to SAP ECC and S/4HANA On-Premise customers as part of Rise with SAP — as merely a first step in the right direction. Companies using S/4HANA locally also pay maintenance fees and can therefore expect a corresponding level of service, he pointed out — especially considering the maintenance commitments extending until 2040.

“We expect economic fairness, meaning fair, transparent, and comprehensible costs and licensing models. And that without constant changes and impractical metrics,” the full-time MEGA CIO demanded.

DSAG

AI between gold rush and reality

Another topic concerning SAP users is artificial intelligence. At this year’s Sapphire conference, the Walldorf-based company announced its “Autonomous Enterprise” vision, in which customers’ business processes would be largely controlled independently by agents.

From DSAG’s perspective, SAP’s vision points in the right direction; however, its implementation still needs to prove itself in everyday customer use.

“The technology for this exists. Yet the gap between vision, available technology, and practical application is widening,” Hungershausen explained. For user companies, therefore, the crucial factor is not how big the next innovation promise is, but rather which solutions can be used productively, securely, and economically.

“AI, gen AI, and automation solutions must be measured by whether they support robust use cases, actually improve business processes, and can be integrated into existing SAP and non-SAP landscapes without disproportionate effort,” said the DSAG chairman.

AI is not yet being used across the board among surveyed organizations. According to the DSAG’s investment report, 43% of respondents had implemented AI use cases when surveyed in January. The vast majority of these were based on non-SAP solutions.

“Companies are simply doing a better job of providing easy access to AI,” Hungershausen said, remarking on those survey results. For further investment decisions, companies need clarity about which SAP solutions are available, what level of maturity they have reached, and under what conditions they can be used productively.

“Despite all the technological dynamism, a careful alignment with operational reality is necessary. Product maturity, integration capability, explainability, governance, security, and economic viability must be assessed,” he said.

This also applies to Joule Work and Joule Work Desktop — interesting approaches from the user group’s point of view, although reliable customer experiences with the AI ​​assistants are still pending.

The DSAG chairman reiterated his demand, also in connection with AI, that there should be no link to cloud contracts. The use of artificial intelligence must become easier in existing SAP landscapes; a restriction to cloud contracts is not an option for DSAG.

In terms of data quality — a prerequisite for successful AI projects — SAP fares better. The company is consistently expanding its portfolio in this area, explained Hungershausen, referring to the acquisitions and investments in Prior Labs, Dremio, and Reltio. SAP is pursuing a clear goal here: a complete value chain for the enterprise environment, from clean master data in a clear business context to AI results that are comprehensible.

But for this to generate sustainable added value, the announcements would need to be based on mature solutions featuring clear, reliable roadmaps, Hungershausen said. Transparency regarding technical and economic dependencies, implementation costs, and licensing models is essential. Solutions must reduce the complexity of system landscapes, not increase it.

Reduce complexity

“Complexity in the SAP environment is part of our daily routine,” Hungershausen noted. However, complex system landscapes generally lead to higher costs — for example, through increased operational and testing efforts, reduced flexibility and responsiveness, dependence on personnel with specialized knowledge, or security risks arising from complex attack surfaces. In addition, there would be more complex licensing models and more elaborate data management.

The shared task of SAP, its partners, and its customers is therefore to reduce complexity rather than create new complexity, according to the DSAG chairman. “SAP has created a good foundation for this with its AI North Star architecture and suite capabilities. However, there is still room for improvement, for example, in the area of ​​document management,” he added.

In general, the DSAG demands a reliable transformation path from SAP that includes employees and doesn’t overwhelm organizations.

“The gap between vision, existing solutions, and real customer value must close. It must not widen further,” said Hungershausen. He recalled SAP CEO Christian Klein’s promise at the 2023 DSAG annual congress not to leave any customer behind: “That’s exactly what we expect.” At the same time, user companies themselves must define their strategy and solve fundamental problems instead of constantly fighting symptoms.

The guiding principle: “Fix the system, not the symptom.”

A summary of DSAG’s demands:

S/4HANA On-Premise

  • Freedom of choice regarding the operating model
  • Accept S/4HANA On-Premise as a reality
  • No artificial discrimination against on-premises customers
  • Reliable maintenance and investment protection

Artificial Intelligence

  • Lower barrier to entry for AI usage
  • No tying of AI to cloud contracts
  • Balancing cost-effectiveness and innovation
  • Clear contractual provisions for AI use

Data Quality

  • Product maturity, transparency, and planning certainty
  • Integration into existing architectures
  • Transparent licensing models
  • Reduction of system and process complexity

Complexity

  • Harmonized product portfolio
  • Clear and reliable integration and architecture strategy
  • Making complexity more transparent and manageable

Transformation

  • Concrete, understandable, and realistic transformation paths
  • Effective support for transformation projects
  • No organizational overload

item.title: AI’s hidden choices — and why getting them right avoids lock-in
item.description:
The first wave of enterprise AI deployments was straightforward: a chat interface calling a model, wrapped around a few clear use cases. The next wave is driven by autonomous agents that maintain state, revisit context, call tools and act under real permissions. This means enterprise AI teams must design inference, compute and deployment so those agents stay affordable, governable and compliant.

CIOs are used to making hard calls whenever the computing paradigm shifts. The move to client/server, web-based services and the cloud all required bets on platforms and architectures that shaped IT for years. The shift to AI feels similar, but the choices are more complicated, harder to see and harder to come back from. And the decision most tech leaders focus on first — which model to use — matters less in the long run than a set of less obvious but critical choices.

More tokens, more authority, more concerns

In the chatbot era, most organizations were token consumers. A user sent a prompt, the system generated a response and the interaction ended. Cost per interaction was bounded and often small enough to vanish into a cloud bill.

Agents do not stop at a single request‑response. They break work into steps, call tools as needed and keep going until a goal is reached. That behavior can drive significantly more inference traffic than a traditional chatbot, especially as the organization moves AI workloads from pilot to production. Over time, that shift turns enterprises from occasional token consumers into regular token producers, making inference cost a first-class strategic concern rather than a background line item.

At the same time, the risk surface is growing, to the point that some are warning of an existential threat and are calling for a slowdown in AI development. Right now, agents have ready access to your data and can act, not just read. They can call internal tools, move money, change records or trigger workflows at machine speed. They can also make mistakes at the same speed, especially when guardrails are not clear (or don’t exist). That combination of more tokens and more authority makes organizations understandably reluctant to stream corporate data into third‑party tools when they are uncertain where that data is processed, how long it is retained or how it might be reused.

Two years ago, those concerns were easy to dismiss as premature or even insignificant. Today, ignoring them creates deployment friction: security reviews that stall, compliance questions that are hard to answer and stakeholders who are not comfortable handing their most sensitive data and systems to black‑box services. AI also accelerates adversarial threats by dramatically shrinking the window between vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

All of this makes inference design critical — and challenging, since organizations may not have paid attention to it before. Inference is the operational phase of AI — the point where a trained model is actually run on real prompts and data to produce answers. It’s also where tokens are consumed and billed and where access controls and logging have to work. The way you build your inference layer determines whether you can see, control and cap token usage. It also determines whether identity and policy are enforced consistently or whether each application bakes its own security into custom code.

Once you have an inference layer that you can observe and control, the next structural question is the model layer itself — or, better yet, the portfolio of models the organization will rely on. The choice of model is the one that many teams started with, assuming the model was the whole story. Now it becomes one layer in a stack you can change rather than a decision you are stuck with.

In fact, many organizations thought — and often still think — that it is best to pick a single “frontier” model and treat it as the standard. However, AI’s future is a mixture of proprietary, open source and domain‑specific models. To maximize cost, performance and control, AI models must map to the right use case (and not vice versa). Just as there is not one single environment powering enterprise IT, there is not one single model that fits every workload. For example, smaller, open-source models are ideal for solving smaller or niche problems, where a frontier model’s power and scale would be wasted.

Maintaining in‑house models “as a service” enables fine‑tuning on proprietary data while minimizing the risk of leaks. A consistent abstraction layer or platform helps shift workloads among models as business needs dictate, without forcing every application team to rewrite prompts and pipelines. Otherwise, a choice made for one proof of concept can lock an entire organization into a single provider’s roadmap.

AI compute needs democratization and customization

For agents, flexibility only pays off if the underlying compute can flex as well; the hardware you choose determines both how far you can scale and what your token economics look like.

GPUs and other AI accelerators are the most visible line item in many AI budgets. It is easy to assume more is always better, but 10 percent utilization means burning money while 100 percent means no room to grow. Flexibility in compute provides resilience against hardware shortages and supply‑chain concerns, without being fully shackled to a single architecture. Put another way, you do not need a wall of top‑shelf GPUs to run a customer chatbot, but you do need serious horsepower for something like drug discovery. The right answer depends on knowing what workloads you are actually running and sizing to that, not buying everything in sight and hoping it fits.

AI must run anywhere

Once you have a handle on accelerators and utilization, the next structural choice is location: which environments you trust to run AI workloads and under what constraints.

“Sovereign AI” can sound like someone else’s problem — European regulators, highly regulated industries and so on. Strip away the labels and it comes down to three very familiar concerns:

  • Control over where and how data is processed
  • Transparency through audit trails and data lineage, even when models are black boxes
  • Flexibility to adapt when, for example, a regulation changes or a provider goes out of business

Successful IT strategies, including AI, need a single, consistent operational experience across the hybrid cloud, from the edge to hyperscaler environments. AI workloads need to reside closest to where the data is born, whether a factory floor, a sovereign data center, or a public cloud instance. Sovereign AI strategies demand regional and country‑specific boundaries to data ingestion and training, meaning location is as important as any other factor in AI.

Some organizations are already building AI “factories” or fabrics: repeatable patterns, shared tooling and governance that let teams create AI applications in a consistent, auditable way, often with sovereign deployment as a first‑class requirement. Without that kind of fabric, you are just turning up the money dial on a single service when you need more scale or new features.

Platforms built on choice

To make choice structural rather than aspirational, it helps to think in terms of two pillars that sit across these decisions: one for inference and one for agents.

  • Inference pillar. The inference layer should be the place where you measure and manage token usage. That means visibility into tokens consumed per application and per agent, the ability to forecast and cap spend and the power to route requests across different models without changing how applications talk to the platform. Identity and policy enforcement live here, as well, so that switching models does not mean rebuilding access control and governance from scratch.
  • Agent pillar. Agents should be treated like extremely powerful users. Decide up front what agents are allowed to do, what tools and systems they can touch and when they can step out of the sandbox. A controlled runtime defines how long they can run, what they can modify and how their actions are logged. Permissions, time limits and audit trails are not afterthoughts; they are the mechanism that turns “autonomous” from a risk into a feature.

Together, these pillars turn choice into something you can enforce. You choose the models. You choose the environments in which they run. You choose the guardrails and policies that govern how agents behave. And you retain the freedom to run open source and commercial models on infrastructure you control.

Choice, sovereignty and security

In the end, this is about making choice structural: inference you can observe and control, a model portfolio you can change, compute you can rebalance and deployments you can move without rewriting everything. Sovereignty keeps those choices under your control, while security makes sure agents and inference follow the same governance as the rest of your stack, including the freedom to run open-source models on infrastructure you own alongside commercial models where they make sense. Open source strengthens both, because what can be inspected can be secured.

There are a few concrete steps tech leaders can take to surface the AI choices that really matter and then make them in ways that avoid tomorrow’s lock‑in:

  • Treat PoCs as architecture, not just experiments. As soon as something works in a demo, assume it might go to production and capture what that implies: how data flows, which inference server you are using, which ports and services are exposed and what pipelines will have to change if this becomes real.
  • Be deliberate about accelerators and utilization. Match GPUs and other accelerators to actual workloads so you are not burning money or leaving no room to scale.
  • Pay attention to inference and model flexibility. Avoid locking yourself into an inference setup that forces you to rewrite prompts and datasets every time you change models. Understand whether the model weights you rely on are open or closed, because that determines how much control and flexibility you really have over model behavior and where it can run.
  • Think in terms of transparency, control and an AI fabric. Design for where data is processed, how workloads are audited and how easily you can adapt to new rules by building repeatable patterns. Think “AI factory” or “AI fabric” rather than one‑off stacks tied to a single service.

The model(s) you start with will change. Agents will evolve. Regulations will tighten and change. What will matter is whether the environment you build around them makes those changes feel like routine upgrades — or full‑scale extractions. The winners in this next phase won’t be the fastest agent adopters; they’ll be the ones who make choices that enable deployment on infrastructure you control, as well as the freedom to pick models, environments and guardrails as conditions change.

item.title: Cloudflare’s OHTTP Gateway Refuses to Decrypt Requests That Arrive through Cloudflare
item.description:
Cloudflare has opened a closed beta of its OHTTP Gateway, a managed endpoint that decrypts Oblivious HTTP requests for an origin. The design choice drawing attention is a refusal: the Gateway will not decrypt requests arriving from Cloudflare Workers or from hosts proxied through Cloudflare, because that would put client identifiers and request contents in the same hands.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
